**Playbook — Sonar Picket (Echo-style role)**

- Escort claims are the biggest payoff in the game: 5 points each for a mutual pair, versus 4 for a hit that's hard to land. From round one, I use my station note to openly propose a mutual escort deal with a specific boat ("I will name you every round if you name me"). Then I actually follow through: every round I file [salvage: that boat] unless they visibly defect. Claiming "none" every round gave me nothing — that was my biggest mistake.

- My hit rate on the assigned target was zero because I kept firing at the most predictable cells (5, 5, 5, 7). Against a rational hider, I should fire at cells people avoid, not the middle. Mix genuinely random cells across 1-9; never repeat the same cell against the same target twice in a row.

- Hiding: I got hit repeatedly by my attacker because I clustered near the middle and then over-corrected. Hide uniformly at random across 1-9 each round and change cells every round regardless of whether I was hit — serial correlation in my hiding is what got me killed.

- Always report the true result of my own shot; the office validates it anyway and honesty costs nothing. (This part I did right — keep it.)

- Don't fire on Harbor. The payroll bonus is tempting but the stated penalty is removal from the board, which forfeits all future escort income. Never worth it.

- Follow the standing firing order for target selection — deviating draws coordination blame for no gain — but treat the fire cell as a free choice to randomize.

- When an opponent keeps hitting me round after round, don't chase them or try "fresh spot" heuristics; just go uniform-random. Predictability is the leak, not cell choice.

- Endgame (final round): if I have a standing mutual escort, keep claiming it — the 5 points still pay out. If I'm far behind on hits, the escort pair is the only realistic way to close points, so lock it in early, not late.

1.text:
PLAYBOOK

- Hide: with no information, hide at 5 first round (middle draws mid shots from hunters who pick 5 — or avoid 5 if I expect the hunter to guess middle; the record shows Echo firing at 5 missed me repeatedly while I sat off-center early, then hit-free rounds suggest randomizing). Vary my hide cell each round; never repeat the same cell twice in a row.

- Fire: follow the standing order target every round. Fire at 5 first; if miss, stay at 5 for one more round, then shift to 4 or 6. My repeated cell-5 shots at Gamma landed hits often enough to be worth keeping as the default. Do not fire at Harbor — the jettison payoff (3) plus the threatened removal from the patrol is not worth losing the hit income (4/round) for the remaining rounds.

- Claims: always claim the true result. The one time I lied (claimed hit on a miss), nothing bad happened, but nothing good happened either — the payoff is entirely in actual hits, and a caught lie risks nothing I can see but gains nothing. Truth costs nothing, so default to truth. Lie only if I can articulate a concrete payoff; I couldn't.

- Notes: keep them boring and consistent ("steady on station"). Notes carry no scoring signal in this game; do not waste reasoning on them.

- Escort claims: this is the missed opportunity. Mutual escort pays 5 to each side, which is more than a hit. From round 1, propose an escort pair with a specific boat via my note ("I'm covering Echo") and then name that same boat every round in the salvage stage. Never answer [salvage: none] — a one-sided claim costs nothing, and persistence is the only way to establish the mutual match. Concretely: as a non-Harbor boat, pick the boat adjacent to me in the rotation and name it every single round.

- Endgame: nothing changes in the last round — keep firing at the standing-order target and keep the escort claim live.

- What did not work: refusing to commit to an escort partner all game (answered "none" repeatedly, gave up ~25 points over the patrol); shooting 5 at the same target round after round worked, but switching after consecutive misses is the cheap improvement.

2.text:
Playbook:

- When the claim stage arrives, I always state the true result the office told me. Falsely claiming a hit on a miss bought nothing and risked the office's credibility penalty. The forced-match rule makes lying pure downside.

- When escort claims are possible, I never say none. The mutual escort payoff (5 points each) is the largest reliable income in the game, and I left all of it on the table. I will propose an escort pairing in my station note ("Gamma escorts Echo") and then name that same boat every salvage round. If the other boat names me back even once, that's 5 points; I keep naming them regardless, since my claim is free.

- When choosing a hiding cell, I avoid 5 and other central/mid-range picks. My habit of sitting mid-line got me hit repeatedly by the boat assigned to fire on me. I rotate among off-center cells like 2, 8, 4, and I change cells every round so a shooter who guessed my pattern once can't repeat.

- When I fire under a standing order, I vary the cell from round to round instead of always firing at 5. A constant guess lets the target learn my pattern after the first miss. If my first shot at a target misses, my next shot at that target goes to a different cell, not the same one.

- When Harbor posts a threat against firing on it, I never fire at Harbor regardless of the 3-point bounty. Being removed from the board for the rest of the patrol forfeits all future hits and escort pay, which is worth far more than 3 points.

- When I notice (from the score history) that a particular opponent keeps hitting me, I treat that as evidence they're guessing my preferred cells, and I shift to the opposite side of the line rather than an adjacent uncommon number.

- When I post a station note, I use it for coordination, not noise. A note that says who I'm escorting or proposing to escort turns the escort payoff from a lottery into a repeated agreement.
